content: Policymakers, healthcare professionals, and community members in lowerand middle-income countries recognize the need to improve access to HIV treatment and ensure patients remain in treatment programs. One proposed strategy involves shifting the delivery of antiretroviral therapy (ART) from hospitals to smaller, more peripheral health facilities or even to community-based settings. This approach has the potential to expand access to care, improve health outcomes, and enhance retention in treatment programs. However, there are concerns that providing care at less sophisticated levels of the healthcare system or at the community level might compromise the quality of care and lead to poorer health outcomes. To address these uncertainties, research studies were reviewed to evaluate the risks and benefits of decentralizing ART service delivery. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of various models of decentralizing HIV treatment and care to more basic levels of the healthcare system, both for initiating and maintaining ART. A comprehensive search was conducted to identify all relevant studies, regardless of language or publication status, from January 1, 1996, to March 31, 2013. The search terms included decentralisation, down referral, delivery of health care, and health services accessibility. Relevant organizations and researchers were also contacted to identify additional studies. The inclusion criteria for the review were controlled trials (both randomized and non-randomized), controlled before-and-after studies, and cohort studies (prospective and retrospective) that involved HIV-infected individuals who were either initiated on ART or maintained on therapy in a decentralized setting in lowerand middle-income countries. Decentralization was defined as providing treatment at a more basic level of the healthcare system compared to the comparator. Two authors independently applied the inclusion criteria and extracted data. A framework was developed to describe different decentralization strategies, and studies were grouped according to these strategies. Data were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis. Since loss to follow-up in HIV programs often includes deaths, the primary outcome was defined as attrition, which encompassed both death and loss to follow-up. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE methodology. Sixteen studies met the inclusion criteria, with all but one conducted in Africa. These included two cluster-randomized trials and 14 cohort studies. The findings were as follows: 1. Partial decentralization: When ART was initiated at a hospital and maintained at a health center, there was a probable reduction in attrition (relative risk [RR] 0.46, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.29 to 0.71, based on four studies with 39,090 patients; moderate-quality evidence). This model may also result in fewer patients being lost to care (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.69; low-quality evidence). 2. Full decentralization: When ART was both initiated and maintained at a health center, there was uncertainty regarding the difference in attrition compared to hospital-based care at 12 months (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.02; four studies with 56,360 patients; very low-quality evidence). However, this model probably resulted in fewer patients being lost to care (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.54; moderate-quality evidence). 3. Community-based care: When ART maintenance therapy was delivered at home by trained volunteers, there was probably no difference in attrition at 12 months compared to facility-based care (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.46; two trials with 1,453 patients; moderate-quality evidence). The authors concluded that decentralizing HIV care aims to improve patient access and retention in treatment programs. Most of the data came from high-quality cohort studies, but the possibility of confounding between the site of treatment and outcomes cannot be ruled out. The review found that partial decentralization, where ART is initiated at a hospital and continued at a health center, appears to reduce attrition. In models where ART is both initiated and maintained at health centers, no significant difference in attrition was observed, but fewer patients were lost to care. For ART provided at home by trained volunteers, no differences in outcomes were detected when compared to facility-based care.
